opus-5.5.text:
I think they're worth something, but probably not in the way people often use them. I wouldn't treat the median answer as a forecast in the sense of "this is when it will happen." What the surveys tell you more reliably is what the people building the technology believe, and how uncertain they are. That's valuable information even if any individual estimate isn't.

For one thing, the answers are noisy and very sensitive to framing. We've seen that asking essentially the same question in slightly different ways, say asking when machines will be able to do all tasks versus when all occupations will be automated, can produce answers decades apart. That tells you people haven't worked out a stable, careful model of this, and you shouldn't take any single number too literally.

But I don't think that makes them useless. AI researchers aren't specialists in forecasting, but they're the people closest to the technology, and I don't know of an obviously better group to ask. If you want to know whether experts think this is far off, whether they think it could go badly, and whether that's a fringe view or a common one, surveys are a decent way to find out. A big part of why I find them useful is that they correct misconceptions. People sometimes assume that concern about catastrophic outcomes from AI is held by a handful of outsiders, and then you ask thousands of researchers and find that a substantial fraction put real probability on extremely bad outcomes. That's important to know, whatever you think about the precision of the numbers.

Then there's the uncertainty itself. When the answers are so spread out, the wide distribution is the finding. It suggests nobody should be very confident that transformative AI is far away, or that it's imminent. And it's useful to track how answers change over time. If the same population, asked similar questions, moves its estimates substantially earlier, that's a meaningful signal even if the absolute levels are off.

So my view is: weight them modestly as forecasts, take them fairly seriously as a picture of expert opinion, and pay close attention to the inconsistencies, because the inconsistencies are also telling you something.

r001.rationale: The response says surveys are valuable despite unreliable individual estimates, but it does not state that the forecasts help people make decisions about AI.

r002.rationale: The response says surveys reveal what researchers believe and whether views are common or fringe, but it does not say that knowing these beliefs helps coordination.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say I place a moderate amount of value on them, but it's worth being clear about what kind of value that is. I don't think the survey forecasts are good as point predictions. When we ask researchers when they expect high-level machine intelligence, the answers vary enormously, and we've seen that small changes in how you frame the question shift the median by decades. So if someone says "experts think it's 2047," I'd want them to hold that quite loosely.

What I do think the surveys are good for is telling you something about the distribution of opinion among people who are close to the work. That's informative even if each individual isn't a reliable forecaster. If a large fraction of researchers think there's a meaningful chance of extremely bad outcomes, that's a fact about the field that matters for policy, regardless of whether their timelines are accurate. It also lets you track how views are changing over time, which has been striking in recent years, because the expected dates have moved forward a lot.

The other thing I'd say is that the alternative isn't some much better source of forecasts. Nobody has a great method here. Expert surveys, trend extrapolation, prediction markets, and inside-view arguments about the technology all have serious problems. I'd treat the surveys as one input, probably more useful for understanding what the community believes and for setting a rough prior than for pinning down specific years.

r001.rationale: The response says surveys can inform policy by showing researchers’ views on catastrophic risk, but it does not clearly state that researchers’ best-guess forecasts are valuable for decisions even when expected to be inaccurate.

r002.rationale: The response describes surveys as revealing the distribution of opinion, but does not say that knowing what people genuinely believe helps coordination.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re useful, but I wouldn’t put a huge amount of weight on them as precise predictions. AI researchers have relevant expertise about what’s happening in their field, but that doesn’t necessarily make them good at forecasting how the whole thing will unfold over decades.

Part of the value is just finding out what people actually think. You often hear claims that AI researchers believe some particular thing, and a survey lets you check whether that’s true, or whether there’s actually a very wide range of views.

I’d also distinguish between taking the dates literally and taking the uncertainty seriously. If researchers give substantial probability to very consequential developments happening relatively soon, that seems worth paying attention to, even if you don’t think they can reliably tell you the year. So I’d treat these surveys as one input into your thinking, rather than something that settles the question.

r001.rationale: The response calls the surveys useful and says to treat them as one input into thinking, but it does not state that the forecasts are valuable for making decisions about AI.

r002.rationale: The response says surveys can reveal what people believe and the range of views, but it does not connect that knowledge to coordination.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re useful evidence, but I wouldn’t take them as authoritative predictions. AI researchers have a lot of relevant knowledge about what’s happening in their field, but that doesn’t necessarily make them good at forecasting how the whole thing will develop over decades.

One reason to do surveys is that otherwise we tend to hear from a few particularly vocal people, and it’s hard to know how representative they are. A survey can tell us something about the broader distribution of views, including how much disagreement there is.

But the answers are also sensitive to how you ask the question. People don’t necessarily have a single, carefully worked-out forecast that they’re reporting. So I’d treat the results as one input into thinking about the future, with substantial uncertainty, rather than as a date we should expect AI to arrive.

r001.rationale: The response calls the forecasts useful evidence and one input to thinking about the future, but does not say they help make AI decisions despite being expected to be inaccurate.

r002.rationale: The response says surveys reveal the distribution of views and disagreement, but does not state that knowing people’s genuine beliefs can help coordination.
